title: The Groan Cup
pitch: A velvet-curtain comedy club where the visitor referees a knockout cup of invented one-liners, picking the funnier of two over and over. Behind the curtain the page fits a Bradley-Terry ranking after every vote, chooses the next pairing that teaches it the most, and then pits the visitor's leaderboard against a panel of silly rule-based judge bots (the pun counter, the length snob, the vowel enthusiast). The payoff is a shareable verdict card: how stable your taste is, which jokes were glazed in the kiln, and which judge bot thinks most like you.
whyNow: A 2026 preprint on tournament-style humor ranking (pairwise judgments aggregated with Bradley-Terry, with adaptive Swiss pairing) is the fresh hook; the mechanic itself is timeless. Humor is owed this week.

research.summary: A 2026 arXiv preprint (HumorRank) ranks humor generation by running theory-informed pairwise preference judgments in a tournament and aggregating them with Bradley-Terry estimation, using adaptive Swiss pairing and checking rank stability with Kendall tau between independent judges. The page rebuilds only that ranking intuition with human votes on a small bundled set of original, invented one-liners; it reproduces none of the paper's results and shows no model scores. Bradley-Terry itself is standard, well-documented background (strength scores from pairwise wins, closely related to Elo, needs a connected comparison graph), so the in-browser fit (an iterative maximum-likelihood update) is honest and small. Paper-specific details come from one paper seen through arXiv and a mirror and stay marked unverified.

title: Dead Rubber Detective
pitch: The visitor is handed the last round of a four-team hockey group, two games played at once, and has to work out which of the two matters, to whom, and whether both teams would quietly settle for an overtime. An exact solver enumerates every result of the two games, sorts each match into stakeless, asymmetric, collusive or competitive, and shows the proof; then the visitor tweaks the standings or the points rule (NHL-style loser point versus the 3-2-1-0 scale used in international hockey) to create a scandal-proof final round, or to engineer the juiciest loophole.
whyNow: The NHL 2026-27 season is a week and a half old and is the first 84-game schedule since 1993-94, so how points and playoff races work is in the conversation; the underlying 2026 match-classification preprints are fresh and one targets low-scoring sports like hockey.

research.summary: Recent arXiv work (2026) classifies matches in the last round of a group by incentive: stakeless (neither prize depends on other results), asymmetric (one side's does not), collusive (both depend on other results yet one outcome secures both), competitive otherwise. One 2026 preprint targets low-scoring sports, which fits hockey, and another studies four-team round-robin last rounds, the exact toy format. The page implements the deterministic classification by brute-force enumeration of a hand-made fictional group, which is small enough to run instantly, and adds a clearly labelled hockey twist (overtime-point rules) that is the page's own extension, not a result from the papers. The NHL 84-game 2026-27 schedule is confirmed by multiple outlets and gives the current hook; the page bundles no real standings.

title: Commute Or Else
pitch: Each day deals a rack of seven operator tiles (add chips, add mult, multiply mult, echo the previous two tiles, mirror a neighbour, raise mult to a power) plus one immovable bedrock tile, and you slide them into the order that scores highest. A live score tree shows chips and mult after every tile, then a histogram of all 5,040 possible orderings reveals where your arrangement sits in a wildly long-tailed distribution, and an exact solver tells you the par. The delight is the first time you see one swap turn 400 into 4,000, and the palindrome rule that rewards symmetric racks.
whyNow: Timeless: ordering effects in chips-times-mult scoring are a perennial talking point among deckbuilder players, and a daily seeded puzzle with a shareable result grid keeps the page worth revisiting.

research.summary: Community guides on deckbuilder joker order agree on the shape of the maths: effects resolve left to right, flat mult belongs before multiplicative mult, and copy effects care about position (one copies its right neighbour, another copies the leftmost slot). That is exactly a non-commutative algebra, (c+a)*b differs from c*b+a, which I derived myself and will self-check in node. The number of orderings of eight items is 8! = 40320 per several counting references, so a rack of 7 movable tiles plus one fixed tile (5,040 orderings) is small enough for exact enumeration in a worker in milliseconds and big enough to have a fat-tailed score distribution worth drawing. Several community claims (exact examples, edge cases for scoring-triggered effects) were contradicted by one forum user, so the page uses its own stated rules, invented tile names and does not claim to reproduce any commercial game.

title: Synergy Overflow
pitch: You are the founder of an invented company pitching buzzword cards to a very gullible board: some add headcount, some add hype, some multiply it by synergy, and a few raise it to a power called disruption. Targets grow like an idle game's cost curve, order matters, and by quarter twenty the numbers have names nobody learned, until the page finally overflows into a deliberate, theatrical NaN-e-Inf board meeting. The joke is the deadpan corporate voice, the payoff is watching the maths run out of numbers.
whyNow: Timeless satire of numbers-go-up design and corporate buzzword inflation; it also fills the owed humor slot with a real mechanic rather than a one-liner.

research.summary: Incremental and idle games rest on a simple recipe: costs rise exponentially (a growth factor of 1.15 per purchase is the convention popularised by one famous clicker, per an analysis paper and a developer write-up) while income rises more slowly, so designers tune payback time and reset with prestige. The deckbuilder community has a famous joke ending: scores that exceed double precision display as a garbled overflow word, with an endless-mode wall and mods that push the cap far higher. That pairing, exponential targets plus an overflow punchline, is a real mechanic with a built-in comedic ending. The satire targets generic corporate speak with an invented company; no real firms or people.

title: Over Your Shoulder
pitch: An essay about attention opens with a doorbell; how long and how rhythmically the visitor presses it is the page's first guess at them. As they read, the page quietly measures dwell time per paragraph, scroll reversals, pointer stillness and tab-aways, then shows a hedged margin note ('you slowed down here, about 60 percent sure') and rewrites later paragraphs to mirror the reader: shorter for skimmers, echoing for re-readers, footnoted for lingerers. It ends with a generated reading portrait and a shareable hash, and the fun is performing as a different reader on purpose to collect all the portraits.
whyNow: Timeless. Form-breaking early-web spirit: the interface is the content, and the rule (the page adapts to how you read it, nothing leaves the device) is felt within ten seconds.

research.summary: Net art of the 1990s made the browser's own layers the subject: JODI projects expose code and fake error screens as primary content, and one 1998 piece redirects the browser so its history list becomes a visible pattern. Modern weird-web examples react to the viewer (blink-triggered warping, text that scrambles under the mouse), but I found none that reads reading itself and rewrites the essay accordingly. The honest science: a CHI 2012 eye-tracking study (36 subjects, 32 tasks) found cursor and gaze only sometimes align, with reading, hesitating and scrolling meaning different things. So the page will present its inferences as hedged guesses and admit when it is wrong, which becomes part of its voice.

title: Tolls In Kind
pitch: A short, sincere essay about how web pages learned to charge for attention sits behind a run of toll gates, and none of them take money. Each gate asks for payment in kind (patience, dignity, spare seconds, a held-still cursor) behind a sign that lies in one specific, learnable way: a decline button worded as a guilt trip, a price list that quietly inverts, fine print that is the real exit. Spot the rule and the toll drops; misread it and the price rises. Each cleared gate unlocks the next paragraph and a codex card naming the trick, and the run ends with an itemised receipt and a daily seed to compare.

title: Drift Harp
pitch: A harp of plucked strings that you strum by dragging a finger or cursor across them, each string a physically modelled Karplus-Strong string tuned in pure just intonation on a live 3-by-5 lattice. Play a looping chord progression and hear and see the pitch creep up by a syntonic comma (about a fifth of a semitone) every lap, a trick called a comma pump. A tempering dial lets you squeeze the drift shut and hear exactly what equal temperament trades away.
whyNow: Timeless: a tuning-system explorer where the surprise is audible. The visitor discovers on their own that pure intervals do not close a loop, which most explainers only state in words.

research.summary: A comma pump is a repeating progression whose pure intervals almost, but not exactly, return to the start, so the pitch shifts by a tiny interval each lap. The standard case is the syntonic comma (81:80, roughly 21.5 cents) in the progression C G D A E C. A 5-limit just intonation lattice puts fifths (3/2) on one axis and major thirds (5/4) on the other, and a loop around the lattice that does not close is the drift made visible. Karplus-Strong gives a cheap plucked string: a short noise burst circulating in a filtered delay line, where loop length sets pitch and the in-loop averaging filter sets decay and brightness. That fits an AudioWorklet or a ScriptProcessor-free delay-buffer implementation with several voices. Browser Karplus-Strong instruments exist, which de-risks the sound engine, but none found combines it with a drifting lattice.

title: Memo Teleprinter
pitch: Type or paste any office memo and a clattering fictional teleprinter turns it into a five-voice rhythm: each letter's 5-bit teleprinter code lights five tracks, and buzzwords from a bundled jargon bank trigger absurd stabs and fanfares. A Euclid dial re-spaces the notes as evenly as possible and the 'cc' list cascades the memo down through ever more bureaucratic echoes. Every memo has its own groove; export the link and send your boss a tune.
whyNow: Timeless office-satire with a mechanic that is genuinely musical: five-bit character codes naturally map to five parallel gates, and Euclidean spacing turns gibberish into something that grooves.

research.summary: Teleprinter codes of the telegraph era used five bits per character, with two shift codes switching between letters and figures; that gives 32 patterns, a ready-made mapping from text to five parallel on/off tracks. Euclidean rhythms, described by Toussaint in 2005, distribute k onsets over n pulses as evenly as possible and reproduce dozens of traditional timelines, for example E(3,8) the tresillo; they come from an algorithm devised for timing neutron beams that mirrors Euclid's greatest-common-divisor method. Combining the two lets typed text drive rhythm and then be re-spaced by an Euclid control. The humour comes from invented, harmless office jargon and a mock-solemn teleprinter persona; no real company, person or brand is used.

title: Between Periods
pitch: It is intermission and the rink is a wreck: skate grooves, divots, and one seeded mishap such as a shower of hats or a split water tank. The visitor steers a small ice-resurfacing machine on a 2D rink, laying shave, wash and squeegee passes so that every scar is covered before the buzzer while a limited water tank empties. The finished sheet gleams, and the result becomes a polished postcard of your own lap pattern that friends can race as a ghost via the link.
whyNow: The 2026-27 hockey season is underway (opened Sept. 29, 2026), so rink lore is in the air, but the mechanic (coverage routing under a turning-radius limit, with a daily rink) works all season and beyond.

research.summary: Two threads shape the design. title: Smudged Memos
pitch: A clerk at an invented Bureau of Misplaced Things receives sealed memos in cipher, each one an absurd grievance built from a hand-written grammar, with a spilled-tea mishap blotting some letters. The visitor works a bench of frequency charts, repeat finders, shift wheels and crib-dragging to crack it, without being told which cipher family it is. Then they can forge a memo of their own from the grammar, pick a cipher and a blot level, and send the link, which carries a sealed envelope that only the recipient can open.

research.summary: Real cryptanalysis supplies the depth: repeated ciphertext fragments of three or more letters hint at the key length of a polyalphabetic cipher (Kasiski), the index of coincidence compares letter-pairing odds against English-like text to test key lengths, and once the length is known each column falls to frequency analysis. That gives a legitimate toolkit the player can use, and it scales from a shift cipher to a short keyword cipher. On the sharing side, daily puzzles commonly use a result grid or card that hides the answer, a pattern the sources describe for Wordle-style games. Putting state in the URL fragment is practical, and a source notes that anyone holding the link can read it, so the sealed memo is deliberately a puzzle, not a secret. All memo text is generated from a bundled grammar of invented, harmless office grievances; nothing is user-typed free text.

title: Sin Bin Concierge
pitch: You run the penalty box as a tiny, deadpan hotel: guests arrive with minors, double minors, majors and misconducts, goals go in, whistles blow, and you must announce who checks out and what the strength on the ice is, before the clock runs out. A real rules engine decides the right answer, including the awkward cases like coincidental minors, a goal on a stacked kill, and a major that refuses to leave early.
whyNow: Timeless, but the 2026-27 season is only two weeks old, penalty-heavy early games are in the news, and a faithful penalty-clock puzzle is the kind of rule detail fans argue about; it is a humor entry that rewards learning real rules.

research.summary: Hockey penalty expiry is a small state machine with surprising edge cases. A minor ends early when the power-play team scores; a major runs its full five minutes regardless; a double minor is two consecutive two-minute blocks, and a goal cancels only the block currently running; coincidental minors in the NHL produce four-on-four play and a goal does not release them. Sources found are general explainers and an older rulebook excerpt, so the spec phase must confirm wording against the current official NHL rulebook, and unconfirmed rules are shown as a simplified house version. The 2026-27 season has few penalty-rule changes (a new neck-protection requirement and an 84-game schedule were reported), so the engine does not depend on news.

title: Certain About Clouds
pitch: A bureaucratic inspection machine looks at cloud-like blots (procedural, or painted by the visitor) and announces what they are with 99-percent-plus certainty: a lighthouse, a nomad, a parade float. Its reasoning transcript is delightfully wrong but fully deterministic, so the visitor can learn its rulebook by predicting its verdicts before it speaks, then try to build a blot that forces it to say a chosen word. The fun is the moment you can finish its sentence.
whyNow: Timeless. Confident machine verdicts are a permanent cultural joke, and this one swaps randomness for a rulebook that rewards understanding.

research.summary: Pareidolia (seeing faces or objects in random patterns) and its umbrella term apophenia give the machine's one big delusion. Classic expert systems (rule base, inference engine, explanation facility that replays which rules fired) give the structure: a forward-chaining rulebook with a printed reasoning trace is both historically real and ideal for a learnable joke. Research on model calibration (stated confidence versus real accuracy) gives the comic law: this machine's certainty is a fixed function that ignores contradicting evidence. Existing confidently-wrong chatbot parodies appear to rely on a language model and randomness; a deterministic, learnable machine is a different experience.

title: Breaking Changes
pitch: A plain grey brick-breaker ships as v0.1. Between waves the studio offers two release candidates written in marketing-speak, such as 'Improved ball responsiveness' or 'Ceiling deprecated to improve performance'. You decode the euphemism, pick one, and play the next wave under its real rules while a board of system lamps shows what just went offline. A codex records what each phrase actually meant, and by v1.0 your build is a loud, glorious, thoroughly broken thing you assembled yourself.
whyNow: Timeless premise, since everyone has met a vague update note, with a jam-weekend nod: one jam page reportedly lists 'Systems Offline' as its theme (as of 2026-10-11, per itch.io, unconfirmed), and each patch here switches a game system off or on.

design.coreLoop: Wave loop: you read two patch notes, pick one with 1 or 2 (or a tap), watch the system-lamp board change as its true effect applies, then play a 30 to 40 second brick-breaker wave under every rule accumulated so far. Clearing the wave or losing a ball ends the loop with a 'known issues' reveal that tells you what the euphemism really meant and files it in the codex. Notes follow a learnable grammar (improved means faster with a catch, rebalanced means nerfed, deprecated means removed with compensation, reimagined means shuffled), so minute two is decoding and minute ten is routing synergies, such as a sticky paddle with gravity, around your build's weak spots. Ten waves end in a v1.0 launch card; three rollbacks end the run early. The daily seed makes the offers identical for everyone.
sophisticationHooks: A decodable grammar: eight verbs (improved, rebalanced, streamlined, reimagined, modernized, deprecated, added in beta, fixed) act on eight game systems (ball, paddle, ceiling, bricks, gravity, input, audio, juice), so a euphemism means the same kind of change everywhere. A codex fills in as you learn, which is what separates minute two from minute ten.

Generic modifier engine with synergy and clamps: about 40 valid verb-noun pairs stack, such as a sticky paddle with gravity or multiball with the ceiling deprecated, while a stall watchdog ships an in-fiction hotfix if no brick falls for 25 seconds.

The juice ladder: feedback layers (hit-stop, squash and stretch, trails, particles, shake, synthesized sound) arrive as patches, so the page shows game feel being built from silent grey boxes at v0.1 to a bright, noisy v1.0. Each layer has a reduced-motion twin and a shake toggle.

Hero moment: a board of system lamps clicks off or on when a patch lands, an installing-update wipe sweeps the playfield, and the same bricks that were flat grey rectangles burst into confetti by v1.0 while the changelog scrolls alongside.
design.scopeForOneDay: Build: fixed-step brick-breaker with sub-stepped collisions, a verb-by-noun patch engine (8 verbs, 8 systems, about 40 valid pairs) with flavor text, two-card picker, system-lamp board, codex, juice ladder with reduced-motion twins, muted-by-default WebAudio blips, ten waves with rollbacks and a v1.0 launch card, URL-hash seed and share string, keyboard and touch controls, about panel with sources. Cut first: unlockable skins, boss wave, extra brick types. Not built: leaderboards, any backend.
risks: Hook is single-sourced and inconsistent: the page shows 'Systems Offline' as reported on a jam page, as of 2026-10-11, per itch.io (unconfirmed); the game does not depend on it.
Brick-breakers are crowded: distinctness rides on the decodable verb grammar, the codex and the writing, so the spec should protect those before extra polish.
Soft-locks and balance: clamp every parameter, ship an in-fiction hotfix that reverts the last patch if no brick falls for 25 seconds, and let the QA monkey test random builds.
Humor stays generic: invented studio, patches and quotes; aim at the genre of vague release notes, never at a real company or product, and list the forum threads only as sources.
Motion and flashing: cap flashes below 3 per second, give every shake or flash a reduced-motion twin and a shake toggle, start audio muted.
Scope: a generic verb-by-noun engine avoids hand-coding dozens of patches; skins, boss waves and extra brick types are cut first.
